title: AI's third era is persistent coworkers, and product cycles are only three months
dek: OpenAI's product lead Tara Seshan argues that AI products are moving from chat to agents to persistent coworkers, and that building must be calibrated to model capabilities two to three months out; the future of work is steering, not rowing, and the part of writing that is thinking will never be automated.
why: Frontline product management experience, offering practical judgments on model cycles, writing trade-offs, and product marketing fit, with direct reference value for teams building AI products.
who: AI product managers, founders, investors, and engineers who want to know the future shape of work.
skip: You can skip the discussion of craftsmanship at 42:22; it doesn't affect the main thread.

points.h: Build for model capabilities two to three months out
points.body: Tara divides the evolution of AI products into three eras: the first is chat, the second is collaborating with agents, and the third, which is coming, is working with a persistent coworker that can accomplish things alongside you. She stresses that when building products, you should neither base them on current model capabilities nor on predictions of what models will be like in a year, but on what models will be capable of in two to three months, because both extremes lead to failure.

points.h: The future of work is steering, not rowing
points.body: Tara believes the future of work will be more about 'steering' than 'rowing': agents handle execution, humans handle direction. The level of abstraction for steering will get higher and higher, but ultimately humans still need to make decisions with conviction. She emphasizes that even as the level of steering rises, human judgment and accountability at critical junctures remain irreplaceable—this is both a responsibility and a source of value.

points.h: The end state is users not having to choose tools
points.body: Tara explains that ChatGPT's 'work mode' is built on Codex, but the UI is different. The product's north star is to make it so users don't have to choose; the system automatically selects the right tool for the task. She emphasizes that 'done is better than perfect'—get it into users' hands first, then fix based on feedback; fast iteration matters more than polish, and she says 'this is the worst the models will ever be.'

points.h: Codex didn't change; users' perception did
points.body: The host observes that the conversation on Twitter about Claude Code and Codex has shifted over the past few months, with more people leaning toward Codex. Tara responds that the Codex team has always been user-oriented and fast-iterating; the internal way of working hasn't changed, but the market and users are gradually realizing this. She thinks the change is not in the team but in users' perception.

points.h: The part of writing that is thinking should never be automated
points.body: Tara distinguishes between 'writing as thinking' and 'writing as reporting.' She would never automate the former, because it's key to organizing thoughts; the latter she fully delegates to models. She advises writing documents to 70% and then seeking feedback, rather than aiming for perfection. At OpenAI, she still writes a lot of documents, but mainly for herself, because long documents are no longer a signal of depth of thinking.

points.h: Before product-market fit, there is product-marketing fit
points.body: The most important lesson Tara learned at Sutter Hill is that product-market fit is important, but she underestimated 'product-marketing fit.' Before building the product, you should refine the narrative and positioning through a lot of selling. She believes excellent product marketing can determine a company's success or failure, and mentions that Mike Speiser is unmatched in this regard.

terms.def: An AI agent that works alongside you over the long term and proactively completes tasks, as opposed to one-off chat or short-term agents.
The degree to which a product's narrative and positioning match the needs of a market segment, emphasizing early refinement of positioning through selling.
